extracted.intended_audience: researchers and advanced students in philosophy of mathematics, mathematicians interested in proof theory and automated deduction, and automated deduction researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply the paper's criteria for valuing and explaining mathematical proofs, focusing on features of methods and inferential steps that make proofs intelligible, explanatory, or otherwise valuable beyond mere correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness/Warrant of Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary traditional role of a proof: to warrant the truth of the resulting theorem (i.e., show that the conclusion follows from the hypotheses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is necessary but not sufficient; many of the other virtues discussed take this as given. The paper contrasts this baseline epistemic role with additional evaluative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory Power (providing understanding beyond truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is valued when it augments our understanding of the theorem, providing a better sense of why the theorem is true (sometimes called 'explanatory').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanatory proofs may show the relevance of particular operations or structures, clarify why certain objects appear, or make the connections that render the theorem intelligible. The paper stresses that explanations can be multiple and context-dependent; it uses 'explanatory' gingerly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality / Strength of Statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that establish stronger or more general statements (from which the original theorem follows) are valuable because they broaden applicability and can subsume the original result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger statements may be appreciated even if they don't alter the original theorem's truth; they can provide insight into a family of related results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of Methods / Uniform Applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods exhibited by a proof are valued when they are powerful and generally/uniformly applicable to other problems and contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powerful methods make it easy to follow complex chains of inference and can be reused to tackle different problems (examples: Gauss sums, algebraic methods used by Dedekind-Weber). The paper argues that some value judgments about proofs are derivative of judgments about the methods they employ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informational Content Beyond Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof can be valuable for conveying information other than mere truth—for instance, indicating how to find constructions, factors, or algorithms tied to the theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proofs that show a method for finding a factor of 2^32+1, or proofs that explain 'why 6' in the Ramsey example. Such proofs answer closely related problems (decide, find witness, prove) and thus supply different kinds of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational/Algorithmic Informativeness (constructive content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how a proof yields explicit computational information or algorithms (i.e., constructive versus nonconstructive proofs and degrees of salience of the constructive content).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper distinguishes being constructively valid from how explicitly a proof makes computational content available. There are degrees: a nonconstructive proof may still yield an 'easily obtained' algorithm; constructive proofs may or may not make witnesses or procedures explicit. References to program extraction and proof theory illustrate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness vs Tedium (economy of calculation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that reduce tedious calculation or number of computation steps are often preferred; concision in computations can be valuable in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a straight calculation proving compositeness can be optimal in some contexts, but proofs that reduce tedious arithmetic (e.g., via congruences) are often superior for human understanding. Counting computation steps relative to 'basic' operations can be used to evaluate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuity / Clarity of Presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that present ideas clearly and make inferential steps easy to follow (i.e., make it straightforward to see that conclusion follows from premises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation, rearrangement of algebraic manipulations, and judicious encapsulation into lemmas/definitions can remove 'clutter' and increase perspicuity (e.g., use of congruence notation). The paper emphasizes intelligibility of small inferential steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestiveness for Discovery / Heuristic Value
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that show how one could have discovered the result in practice, i.e., supply heuristics or motivation that lead to the proof or construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Euler's proof that explains how he might have hit upon 641. Such proofs are valued because they teach methods of discovery and are pedagogically useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferability and Usefulness in Related Contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods or proofs that transfer to or explain phenomena in broader contexts (e.g., use of Gaussian integers leading to product rules and classification theorems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'capital improvement' viewpoint counts the cost of developing background theory (like norms and algebraic extensions) as paid back by broad utility and explanatory reach; proofs that illuminate connections across areas (e.g., algebraic number theory) are highly prized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to Support Generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that naturally suggest or enable generalizations (e.g., to families of theorems, higher dimensions, or classification results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper gives examples where conceptual proofs lead to structural classification (Hurwitz/Zorn/Frobenius results) and where methods generalize (product rules for sums of squares).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of Definitions and Lemmas (encapsulation/modularity)
rubrics_metrics.description: How information is packaged—definitions and lemmas can encapsulate witnesses and intermediate steps, changing what is visible in the main proof and affecting perceived explanatory power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unwinding definitions can make a proof longer but may reveal hidden structure; conversely, encapsulation can make a proof seem shorter while shifting work into lemmas. This affects what we say the proof explains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation and Presentation Choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of notation and representational devices (e.g., congruence notation, Gaussian integers) that reduce clutter and make structural features apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good notation can hide routine algebraic identities and make key ideas salient; poor notation can obscure methods and require unnecessary computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and Fruitfulness of Concepts/Definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions are valuable when they are 'fruitful'—they facilitate quantificational reasoning, enable transfer of methods, and reveal hidden symmetries or structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper cites Fregean and Tappenden-style discussions: a fruitful definition allows useful quantifier reasoning and promotes conceptual insights (e.g., divisibility, congruence, norm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of Formal/Model-theoretic Adequacy (formalizability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether formal models of deduction (standard logical frameworks) capture the features mathematicians use to evaluate proofs, and whether alternative models (automated deduction frameworks) do better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that standard models of formal deduction are insufficient to make some valued features apparent, and discusses automated-deduction models (and formal proof languages like Isabelle/Isar) as potentially better suited for capturing method-related evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Inferential Structure / Methods of Inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on the small-scale inferential steps (methods of inference) that make a proof intelligible—how tokens detect applicability and how witnesses are instantiated in quantificational reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper emphasizes that understanding lower-level inferential steps matters for assessing intelligibility and explanation, and that methods can be viewed as tokens that detect patterns in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of Abstraction / Implementation-independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuing frameworks that abstract away implementation-specific details while retaining salient method features (i.e., being concrete enough to be informative but not tied to a particular implementation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The challenge is to avoid language that is either too vague or overly specific (implementation-specific), aiming for a framework that preserves the methodological features mathematicians care about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive vs Nonconstructive Character (philosophical/epistemic stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a proof aligns with constructive standards (provides explicit witnesses/algorithms) or is nonconstructive, and how that affects its epistemic and practical value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes mathematical-logic characterizations of constructivity and discusses how even nonconstructive proofs can be interpreted or transformed to yield constructive information (program extraction, proof theory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical and Problem-solving Value
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that help learners find counterexamples, understand heuristics, or solve closely related problems are especially valuable in teaching and problem-solving contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Ramsey proof suggests how to find counterexamples among five people and hints at generalizations; the separation of 'prove', 'decide', and 'find' as different associated problems highlights pedagogical differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory Economy / Why-Answers
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that answer 'why' questions succinctly—explaining the role of particular structures or operations in the theorem rather than only verifying truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper contrasts brute-force verification with proofs that make the relevance of operations (like exponentiation in Fermat-number proofs) manifest, giving a sense of explanatory economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual and heuristic relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof may be judged valuable for the historical or conceptual role it played in developing methods or theory (e.g., introducing new methods that led to further advances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Gauss sums, Dedekind-Weber introducing algebraic methods, and Euler's uses of Gaussian integers; such historical role bolsters judgments about method-value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readable Formal Documentation (structured formal proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human-readable formal proof documents (e.g., Isar/HOL structured proofs) that make formal inferences accessible and show methods at the object level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper discusses formal proof environments and structured proof languages as ways to represent methodological content; readable formalisms can bridge practice and formal models, though choices about libraries and rules influence how much methodological content is captured.
